strengths: Well-motivated problem: Addresses genuine bottleneck in expressive TTS—lack of objective stylistic consistency metrics
Sound methodology: MCLP metric is intuitive and grounded in information-theoretic principles (MI maximization)
Comprehensive experiments: Video-level train/test splits, multiple metrics (CER, WER, MCLP, MOS), thorough ablations demonstrating reward hacking issues
Practical reward design: Hybrid gated reward combining MCLP and CER successfully balances expressiveness and intelligibility, as evidenced by ablation studies
Valuable dataset contribution: 311k scenes (1,435 hours) with systematic annotation pipeline and video-level splits enable future research
Strong empirical results: Significant improvements over baselines (MCLP -4.636 vs -4.829 for Step-Audio-2-mini; MOS 3.646 vs 1.707)
Clear presentation: Generally well-written with informative figures and adequate mathematical exposition
weaknesses: Circular validation: MCLP used as both metric and reward signal; human consistency analysis (Figure 5) evaluates samples optimized to maximize MCLP, creating potential circularity rather than validating metric independence

Unvalidated information-theoretic assumptions: KL divergence term dismissed with 'assuming small'; assumption that MI variation dominated by style attributes never empirically validated; pretrained LALM quality as density estimator not verified
Ground-truth assumption problematic for expressive speech: Single reference audio inadequate when multiple valid stylistic continuations exist; metric may penalize creative valid interpretations

Severely limited human evaluation: Only 31 samples (30 valid) with no inter-annotator agreement reported; only 32 annotators; poor stratification (2 samples for 5+ turns); large confidence intervals (±0.06 MOS); gold standard sample not described

Dataset annotation quality unverified: Scene descriptions from Qwen-VL-7B (visual model), character profiles inferred by DeepSeek-R1; no quality assessment, verification, or noise analysis of LLM-generated annotations

Incomplete ablations: No sensitivity analysis for bias term C, context history construction, MCLP hyperparameters, or gating threshold τ; arbitrary reward parameters (C=15.0, λ=10.0, τ=0.2) lack justification
Limited generalization: All experiments on Mandarin Chinese drama only; unclear transferability to other languages, domains, or speech types; role-play from drama is specific stylistic context
Weak baseline comparisons: Only three LALM baselines, none specifically designed for role-play; missing comparisons with simpler style metrics (speaker similarity, prosody measures)

Reproducibility gaps: Pretrained LALM checkpoint release not mentioned; code not available; TA4 tokenization details sparse; internal classifier training procedures not specified; no statistical significance tests beyond confidence intervals
Ethical concerns underexplored: Minimal impact statement given implications for voice spoofing, deepfakes, and character impersonation

strengths: Addresses a practical and under-explored problem: stylistic consistency metrics for role-play TTS
Reasonable core idea of leveraging LALM likelihood as a style consistency proxy with information-theoretic grounding
Comprehensive ablation studies demonstrating necessity of SFT and RL components and effects of reward hacking
New dataset contribution with ~1,400 hours of multi-turn dialogue role-play speech from real dramas
Clear demonstration of trade-offs between style and content optimization through hybrid reward design
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: MCLP is a straightforward application of log-likelihood averaging; the overall approach (SFT + RL with hybrid rewards) is standard practice
Insufficient subjective evaluation: only 30 valid MOS samples for a top-tier venue (typically requires 50-100+); no statistical significance testing between methods
Weak MCLP-MOS correlation: Figure 5 shows win rate plateaus at 80-90% with noise; correlation only strong for ΔMCLP > 0.1, not universally strong
Dataset annotation concerns: scene descriptions and character profiles generated by LLMs (Qwen-VL-7B, DeepSeek-R1) without human validation; no inter-annotator agreement metrics reported

Suspicious baseline results: Step-Audio-2-mini baseline achieves 12% CER (W/O history) but drops to 1.6% after fine-tuning—10.4% improvement is enormous and suggests unfair comparison or weak baseline tuning
Unverified theoretical assumption: Information-theoretic justification assumes small KL divergence (Eq. 3) but never empirically validates this critical assumption
Arbitrary hyperparameter choices: λ=10.0, C=15.0, τ=0.2, G=8 lack sensitivity analysis or justification; gating threshold τ=0.2 seems harsh and unmotivated
Opaque data curation: RL dataset filtering uses an undescribed 'internal style classification model'; significant attrition (12,541→1,435 hours) without clear justification

Limited scope and generalizability: only evaluated on Chinese drama RP-TTS; unclear how MCLP generalizes to neutral TTS, other languages, or non-role-play stylistic tasks; no comparison with alternative style metrics
Presentation issues: MCLP context formulation H=[w, z_eval, w] lacks motivation for repeating transcript; Figure 1 is dense and difficult to parse; missing pretraining procedure details
RL only applied to final turn in dialogues, limiting practical applicability to multi-turn scenarios; reproducibility concerns due to complex pipeline with multiple external tools
No direct human preference evaluation comparing generated audio between methods beyond limited MOS scores
Ground-truth MOS (4.41) vs. proposed method (3.65) shows substantial gap, raising questions about practical utility

strengths: Novel MCLP metric leveraging LALM in-context learning capabilities with intuitive motivation and reasonable information-theoretic grounding (Eqs. 2-3)
Strong empirical results with substantial improvements over competitive baselines (MOS: 3.646 vs 1.707-2.471; CER: 1.130% vs 3.276-12.007%)
Comprehensive system design with thoughtful hybrid reward combining style (MCLP) and content (CER) objectives and gated aggregation to prevent reward hacking
High-quality large-scale RP-TTS dataset (311k scenes, 1,435 hours) with careful multi-stage annotation pipeline and open-sourcing commitment
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating necessity of SFT, RL, and hybrid reward components; clear evidence of reward hacking with single-objective optimization (Table 3)
Human-metric consistency analysis (Figure 5) showing encouraging correlation between MCLP and MOS with >0.8 win rate at ∆MCLP > 0.1
Clear presentation of methodology with appropriate experimental setup (video-level train/test split to prevent data leakage)
weaknesses: Insufficient justification for why MCLP specifically captures 'style' vs general audio quality/fidelity; assumes variation in mutual information dominated by prosodic attributes but provides no empirical validation of this assumption
Limited validation scope: MOS evaluation uses only 31 samples (30 valid), win rates at ∆MCLP=0.08 are only ~0.6-0.65 suggesting substantial noise or imperfect metric correlation
Generalization concerns: MCLP validated only on Chinese drama role-play TTS; unknown applicability to other languages, genres, speaking contexts, or with different pre-trained LALMs

No comparison with alternative style metrics (emotion classification, prosodic features, speaker consistency) to justify MCLP superiority; missing comparisons with instruction-based TTS methods cited in related work

Dataset annotation quality unvalidated: scene/character descriptions generated by LLMs without inter-annotator agreement; critical 'internal style classification model' for RL filtering not described, introducing potential systematic bias

Key design choices unjustified: RL applied only to final turn without explanation; reward hyperparameters (C=15.0, λ=10.0, τ=0.2) set without sensitivity analysis; binary gating in Eq. 9 potentially unstable near threshold

Information-theoretic justification relies on untested assumptions (small KL divergence in Eq. 3, LALM as strong density estimator); context history design H=[w,z_eval,w] repeats transcript without ablation justifying this choice
Reproducibility barriers: requires 32 H800 GPUs; Step-Audio-2-mini-Base requires 300w hours pretraining; dataset release timeline unspecified; closed-source GPT-Audio baseline
Limited qualitative analysis: no audio samples, spectrograms, or error case studies; no discussion of failure modes; missing comparison with emotion-based RL approaches mentioned in related work

strengths: Novel MCLP metric leveraging LALM in-context learning to quantify stylistic consistency, validated to correlate with human judgments (win rate >0.8 when ΔMCLP >0.1)
Thoughtful hybrid reward design with gating mechanism that effectively prevents reward hacking, demonstrated by ablation showing 61% CER when optimizing only MCLP
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with consistent improvements over strong baselines (1.13% CER vs 3.28% for Step-Audio-2-mini; 3.576 MOS vs 2.484 for MiMo-Audio-7B)
Large-scale WenetSpeech-RP-TTS dataset (311k scenes, 1,435 hours) with systematic annotation pipeline and detailed analysis across scene categories, dialogue lengths, and speaker counts
Thorough ablation studies demonstrating necessity of SFT and RL stages and the contribution of each reward component
weaknesses: MCLP design lacks rigorous justification: the context order [w, z_eval, w, z_gt] is not symmetric despite claims; no ablation comparing alternative formulations; choice of semantic TA4 tokens vs acoustic tokens not principled

Weak validation of annotation quality: character and scene descriptions auto-generated by LLMs with minimal quality control; no correlation study between annotation noise and downstream performance; 'style filtering' using internal classifier is undisclosed

Limited scope severely reduces significance: Mandarin-only with drama domain focus; cross-lingual validation relegated to preliminary 1K-sample experiment on unrelated dataset; no evaluation on audiobooks, games, or other domains acknowledged as future work

Insufficient human evaluation: only 30 test cases with 48 valid annotators after filtering; non-standard MOS scale (0.5-5.0) limits comparability; no formal statistical significance testing; small evaluation set limits statistical power

Baseline fairness concerns: GPT-Audio shows anomalously high CER (11.974% with audio history); unclear if baselines were properly adapted; test set stratification (100 samples per dialogue length from 200 video candidates only) limits diversity

Critical reproducibility gaps: code link is placeholder; RL dataset aggressively filtered (16,186 from 300k scenes) without bias analysis; computational cost of MCLP not reported; internal style classification model undisclosed

Incomplete technical validation: no ablation on gating mechanism or hyperparameter sensitivity; no analysis of MCLP saturation or failure modes; continuation model quality's impact on MCLP not investigated; no comparison to alternative likelihood-based metrics

Theoretical foundation unvalidated: claim that LALMs encode 'continuous latent space of audio styles' is posited but never demonstrated; what style dimensions the continuation model learns remains unexplored

strengths: Addresses a real and practical problem: lack of objective metrics for stylistic consistency in multi-turn RP-TTS
Comprehensive empirical evaluation with multiple metrics, human evaluation with quality control, and fine-grained ablations demonstrating that MCLP and CER rewards complement each other
Clear validation that MCLP aligns with human judgments of stylistic consistency (Figure 5: win rate >80% when ΔMCLP>0.1)
Substantial dataset contribution: WenetSpeech-RP-TTS with ~311k scenes, 1,435 hours from real drama videos with annotated scenes and characters
Strong empirical results outperforming competitive baselines on both objective metrics and subjective MOS (3.576 vs 2.484 best baseline)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: MCLP is a straightforward application of LALM continuation likelihood; no novel insights into metric design or justification for key choices (e.g., why [w, z_eval, w] context ordering?). Design choices lack ablation studies

Critical annotation quality concerns: Scene and character descriptions are automatically generated by LLMs (Qwen-VL, DeepSeek-R1) with unquantified accuracy. No inter-annotator agreement, accuracy statistics, or sample validation provided, undermining reliability of all downstream results

Severely insufficient human evaluation: Only 30 test cases with complex stratification; 48 valid annotators (2% dropout); single gold-standard quality control case; no inter-rater reliability (ICC/Fleiss' kappa) reported. Scale is below standard for drawing strong preferences

Narrow scope with unvalidated generalization: Main evaluation limited to Mandarin Chinese drama only. Preliminary English results (Appendix B) minimal with no analysis. Claimed applicability to audiobooks/games not demonstrated. Cross-lingual generalization completely unvalidated

Aggressive RL data filtering (311k→16k scenes, 94.8% reduction) via turn, length, and style constraints makes it unclear whether improvements come from RL or just high-quality curated data. No isolation of RL contribution

Questionable metric design: (1) MCLP computes z^gt from z^eval but theoretical justification for why backward continuation predicts style consistency is weak. (2) Core assumption that 'LALMs encode latent style space' stated but never validated. (3) Table 3 shows w/o CER still reaches -4.590 MCLP with 61% CER, indicating metric remains gameable. (4) Arbitrary choices (gating threshold τ=0.2, bias term C=15.0) lack justification or sensitivity analysis

Reproducibility failures: Code URL stated but blank. Continuation model trained on '3 million hours' of unspecified source. Cannot reproduce MCLP metric without trained model. No inter-rater reliability data available

Experimental concerns: (1) Step-Audio-2-mini baseline shows 3.276% CER with history but 12% without—poorly tuned or unfair setting? (2) Instruct-TTS baselines cannot use audio history, making comparisons asymmetric. (3) No significance testing between conditions despite small sample sizes. (4) Missing comparison with other recent RL-based TTS (Wang et al. 2025 emotion classification cited but not compared)

Insufficient analysis and insights: No error cases, failure modes, or qualitative examples showing when MCLP works/fails. No analysis of what styles MCLP actually captures (prosody, emotion, rate, acoustic quality?). No simple baseline comparisons (e.g., speaker embedding similarity as reward)

Statistical rigor issues: No significance testing in main results tables. No confidence intervals for MCLP scores. Effect sizes not reported. MOS evaluation lacks standard inter-rater agreement metrics despite being the primary validation

strengths: Novel MCLP metric addresses a real bottleneck in TTS evaluation by leveraging LALM in-context learning to quantify stylistic consistency objectively
Strong empirical validation showing clear alignment between MCLP and human judgments (>0.8 win rate when ΔMCLP > 0.1 in Figure 5)
Well-designed RL framework with thoughtful hybrid reward combining MCLP and CER, including gating mechanism to prevent reward hacking
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple baselines, proper ablations, and fine-grained analysis across scene categories, dialogue lengths, and speaker counts
Large-scale high-quality dataset (WenetSpeech-RP-TTS: 311k scenes, 1,435 hours) with detailed scene and character annotations, providing valuable resource for future research
Solid experimental methodology with video-level train/test splits preventing data leakage and gold-standard annotator quality control
Significant practical improvements: MOS increases from 2.484 (best baseline MiMo-Audio-7B) to 3.576 (proposed), with consistent gains across objective metrics
Reproducible work with detailed training procedures, hyperparameters, and dataset construction pipeline documented in main paper and appendices
Clear positioning distinguishing RP-TTS (stylistic consistency) from recent speech role-playing agents (semantic alignment), addressing underexplored aspect
Honest limitations discussion acknowledging language scope (Mandarin-primary), domain coverage (drama only), and annotation noise from LLM-generated descriptions
weaknesses: Limited language coverage with evaluation primarily on Mandarin Chinese; cross-lingual generalization (Appendix B) is preliminary and should receive greater validation
Theoretical grounding for why continuation likelihood serves as stylistic consistency proxy could be deeper; the connection is intuitive but not rigorously analyzed
Minimal documentation of continuation model training (3M hours) including convergence criteria, validation performance, training stability, and final model quality assessment
Test set comprises only ~0.29% of dataset (900/311k scenes); while stratified sampling is appropriate, larger test set would strengthen statistical confidence in results
Dataset limited to drama genres; broader applicability to audiobooks, games, virtual assistants, and other domains remains unvalidated
Missing ablations on key design choices: no analysis of repeated-transcript component necessity in MCLP context history, and no comparison of alternative context designs
Auto-generated scene/character annotations using LLMs could introduce noise and bias; limited discussion of annotation quality validation or error rates
Instruct-TTS baselines evaluated only in w/o audio-history setting due to architectural constraints, limiting full comparison scope
Hyperparameter choices (C=15.0, λ=10.0, τ=0.2) lack sensitivity analysis or justification of selection methodology
No ablation on LALM model choice; while Step-Audio-2's semantic tokenizer is justified, comparison with other LALM architectures would strengthen the generality claim
